summary: From ape-men to the Star Child: a mysterious monolith drives exploration of space, and the astronaut Bowman survives the murderous computer HAL to pass beyond the infinite.

hunger.why: The ape-men scrape for roots, then learn to kill and eat tapir meat; astronauts eat paste trays and sandwiches.

thirst.why: Two ape tribes fight over the waterhole in the opening sequence.

feeling-cold-hot.why: The African desert and the cold of space are settings, not hardships.

sleepiness.why: Floyd sleeps on the shuttle, three crew hibernate in pods, and HAL kills them in their sleep.

curiosity.why: The moon excavation, the Discovery voyage to Jupiter, and Bowman's passage through the Stargate are driven by exploration.

explanation-seeking.why: What the monolith is, who buried it, why HAL predicts a fault, and what happens beyond Jupiter are the film's unanswered questions.

skill-acquisition.why: The ape-men learn to use bones as tools and weapons after touching the monolith.

play.why: Poole shadowboxes and plays chess with HAL, Bowman sketches; play is marginal.

resource-accumulation.why: No one gains wealth or possessions.

resource-foraging.why: The ape-men forage for food and water and seize the waterhole.

mental-time-travel.why: Bowman and Poole plan HAL's disconnection in the pod, and HAL reads their lips and plans to stop them.

fear-of-predators.why: A leopard kills an ape-man in the dark, and the tribe huddles in fear at night.

fear-of-aggressors.why: Ape tribes battle at the waterhole, HAL murders Poole and the sleepers, and Bowman fights his way back aboard.

fear-of-heights.why: Poole tumbles into the void, weightless corridors spin, and the Stargate plunges through dizzying space.

disgust.why: The tapir carcass and Bowman's aging body hint at decay, briefly.

pain-aversion.why: Poole's air hose is cut, the ape leader is beaten to death, and Bowman risks explosive decompression.

pride.why: HAL boasts of being incapable of error, and Floyd is congratulated on Clavius.

shame.why: HAL's exposed error threatens his self-image of infallibility.

moral-pride.why: Bowman persists in his mission; principled stands are marginal.

guilt.why: HAL admits he has made some very poor decisions as he is shut down.

warmth.why: Floyd's call to his daughter and Poole's parents' birthday message are small, cold kindnesses.

moral-blame.why: HAL's betrayal is wrong, but no one condemns it in words.

moral-praise.why: No one is celebrated for goodness.

revenge.why: The bone-wielding tribe retakes the waterhole by killing the rival leader, and Bowman disconnects HAL after the murders.

compassion.why: Bowman tries to retrieve Poole's body, and HAL pleads for mercy as his mind fades.

friendship.why: Bowman and Poole work as a quiet, trusting pair.

sadness.why: Poole's death and HAL's dying song touch loss only lightly.

humor.why: The zero-gravity toilet instructions and HAL's politeness supply dry comedy.

reasoning.why: Bowman and Poole debate HAL's reliability, and HAL argues his own case.

coalitional-affiliation.why: Rival ape tribes, the Soviet and American scientists, and the crew against HAL form loose sides.

status-seeking.why: The ape-men win dominance over the waterhole with their new weapon.

envy.why: The displaced ape tribe wants the waterhole the others hold.

anger.why: The ape-men scream and fight; anger is otherwise absent from the cool astronauts.

hatred.why: No one takes pleasure in another's suffering.

parental-care.why: Floyd's video call with his small daughter and the Star Child's birth touch on children, briefly.

parental-investment.why: The monolith acts as a teacher to the ape-men, but child-rearing is marginal.

familial-love.why: Floyd's daughter and Poole's parents appear in brief transmissions.
